note:
Dictating a pediatric specialty clinic visit for a 5-year-old female who is here with her mother for right ear pain and fever. History of present illness, the mother says the ear pain started 2 days ago, correction, 3 days ago, right after a cold that had been going on for about a week with a runny nose and a cough. She has been tugging at her right ear, woke up crying twice last night, and had a fever up to 38.6 Celsius at home that came down partly with ibuprofen. She also had a mild sore throat yesterday. She is eating a little less but is drinking fluids well and is passing urine normally. She denies vomiting, diarrhea, neck stiffness, or drainage from the ear, and the mother has noticed no change in her hearing and no rash.

Past medical history includes mild persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, and three ear infections in the last 6 months. The last infection was treated with amoxicillin about 2 months ago, which she tolerated well. She has no known drug allergies. Current medications per the mother are fluticasone HFA 44 mcg 2 puffs twice daily, albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4 to 6 hours as needed, cetirizine 2.5 mg once daily, hydrocortisone 1% cream twice daily to the eczema patches as needed, and diphenhydramine at bedtime that the mother started over the counter last week for the congestion. She had no wheezing episodes this month and has needed albuterol only twice. Immunizations are up to date including the pneumococcal conjugate series, but she has not had the flu shot this season. She attends kindergarten and a classmate had a similar illness. No smokers at home.

Vitals today, temperature 38.4 Celsius, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and weight 20 kilograms, correction, 18 kilograms on the clinic scale. On examination she is tired appearing but consolable and well hydrated. Right tympanic membrane is bulging, erythematous, and opaque with decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, and the landmarks are obscured. Left tympanic membrane is pearly with good landmarks and normal mobility. No mastoid tenderness or swelling and no postauricular erythema. Nose has pale boggy turbinates with clear rhinorrhea. Throat is mildly erythematous without exudate, neck is supple with shallow bilateral anterior cervical nodes, lungs are clear to auscultation with no wheeze, heart is regular without murmur. Skin shows dry patches in both antecubital fossae. Tympanometry showed a flat type B tracing on the right and a normal type A tracing on the left. A rapid strep antigen test done in clinic was negative.

Impression is acute otitis media of the right ear, which is her fourth episode in 6 months and meets criteria for recurrent otitis media. Her asthma is well controlled, her allergic rhinitis is not well controlled and is likely contributing, and the atopic dermatitis is stable. Plan, start amoxicillin 900 mg twice daily for 7 days, correction, 800 mg twice daily for 7 days, which is about 90 milligrams per kilogram per day based on the corrected weight. Use ibuprofen 180 mg every 6 hours as needed for ear pain or fever. Increase the cetirizine from 2.5 mg to 5 mg once daily. Stop the diphenhydramine at bedtime because it thickens secretions and can disturb sleep. Continue the fluticasone, albuterol, and hydrocortisone 1% cream as prescribed. Refer to pediatric otolaryngology to discuss tympanostomy tubes given the recurrent episodes. Recheck in 2 weeks with repeat tympanometry, and arrange an audiology evaluation if the right-sided effusion persists. We recommend the influenza vaccine once she has been afebrile for a few days. Return precautions reviewed with the mother, return sooner if fever persists beyond 48 hours, if there is ear drainage, swelling behind the ear, severe pain, or if she is not drinking well. The mother verbalized understanding. End of dictation.
summary: A 5-year-old female with mild persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis presented with her mother for 3 days of right ear pain and fever after a week-long cold, with three prior ear infections in the last 6 months. Examination showed a bulging, erythematous, opaque right tympanic membrane with decreased mobility, a flat tracing on tympanometry, and a negative rapid strep test. The impression is acute otitis media of the right ear, her fourth episode in 6 months. Amoxicillin 800 mg twice daily for 7 days and ibuprofen were prescribed, cetirizine was increased to 5 mg daily, and diphenhydramine was stopped. Referral to otolaryngology and a 2-week recheck were arranged.

Mild sore throat yesterday. Eating a little less but drinking well and passing urine normally. Denies vomiting, diarrhea, neck stiffness and ear drainage; no change in hearing, no rash, no wheezing this month. History of mild persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis and three ear infections in the last 6 months, the last treated with amoxicillin about 2 months ago and well tolerated. Immunizations up to date; no influenza vaccine this season.

Right tympanic membrane bulging, erythematous and opaque with decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; left tympanic membrane normal. No mastoid tenderness or swelling. Pale boggy turbinates with clear rhinorrhea; throat mildly erythematous without exudate; shallow bilateral anterior cervical nodes; lungs clear; heart regular without murmur; dry patches in both antecubital fossae. Tympanometry flat type B on the right and type A on the left. Rapid strep antigen test negative.
soap.assessment: Acute otitis media of the right ear, her fourth episode in 6 months (recurrent otitis media). Asthma well controlled, allergic rhinitis not well controlled, atopic dermatitis stable.
plan: Start amoxicillin 800 mg twice daily for 7 days (about 90 milligrams per kilogram per day for the corrected weight of 18 kilograms)
Ibuprofen 180 mg every 6 hours as needed for ear pain or fever
Increase cetirizine from 2.5 mg to 5 mg once daily
Stop diphenhydramine at bedtime
Continue fluticasone, albuterol and hydrocortisone 1% cream
Refer to pediatric otolaryngology to discuss tympanostomy tubes
Recheck in 2 weeks with repeat tympanometry; audiology evaluation if the right-sided effusion persists
Influenza vaccine once afebrile for a few days
Return sooner for fever beyond 48 hours, ear drainage, swelling behind the ear, severe pain or poor drinking

note:
Chief Complaint: Fall at home while on a blood thinner.

HPI: 86-year-old male brought in by EMS after a ground-level fall at home earlier this morning. He tripped on the edge of a rug while walking to the bathroom and landed on his left side, striking the left side of his head on the floor. There was no loss of consciousness, and he was able to sit up with help from his daughter, who found him within minutes. He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation and took his morning dose about 2 hours before the fall. He currently has scalp soreness and left forearm pain. Past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Other home medications are metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

ROS: Denies headache, vomiting, neck pain, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness before the fall, new weakness, numbness, or vision changes. No abdominal pain. No shortness of breath.

Physical Exam: Temp 36.8 C, HR 76 and irregularly irregular, BP 148/82, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, weight 58 kg. Alert and oriented, GCS 15. There is a left parietal scalp hematoma of about 3 cm that is tender, with no laceration and no step-off. Pupils are equal and reactive, cranial nerves are intact, strength is 5/5 and symmetric, and there is no pronator drift. Neck has no midline tenderness. Chest wall is nontender and lungs are clear. Heart is irregularly irregular without murmur. Abdomen is soft and nontender. The left forearm has a 4 cm abrasion with mild tenderness over the distal radius, no deformity, and intact sensation and perfusion. Pelvis is stable and both hips are nontender with full range of motion.

ED Course / Results: CT head without contrast showed no intracranial hemorrhage and no fracture, with a left parietal scalp hematoma. CT cervical spine showed no acute fracture. X-ray of the left forearm and wrist showed no fracture. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 78 and no acute ischemic changes. Labs: hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 1.6, potassium 4.2, troponin negative. Because he is anticoagulated, a repeat CT head at 6 hours was obtained and was stable with no delayed bleed. The abrasion was cleaned and dressed. He was given acetaminophen 650 mg once for scalp soreness with good relief and then walked in the department with a steady gait.

Medical Decision Making: Mechanical fall without syncope in an elderly man on apixaban, with a scalp hematoma and a forearm abrasion. Imaging is negative for intracranial hemorrhage and fracture, and the stable 6 hour repeat CT supports safe discharge. He meets dose reduction criteria for apixaban given age over 80, weight 58 kg, and creatinine 1.6, so the dose will be reduced from 5 mg to 2.5 mg twice daily. Fall risk was discussed, and a home safety evaluation is recommended.

Disposition: Discharged home with his daughter. Hold apixaban tonight and resume tomorrow morning at 2.5 mg twice daily. Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain, and avoid NSAIDs. Continue metoprolol succinate and lisinopril. Return for headache, vomiting, confusion, drowsiness, or new weakness. Follow up with his primary care physician in 1 week, with home physical therapy and a home safety evaluation arranged.
summary: An 86-year-old male on apixaban for atrial fibrillation was brought in after a ground-level mechanical fall at home, striking the left side of his head without loss of consciousness. He had scalp soreness, a 3 cm left parietal scalp hematoma and a forearm abrasion. CT of the head and cervical spine, a forearm X-ray and an ECG showed no acute injury, and a repeat head CT at 6 hours was stable. The impression is a mechanical fall without syncope with minor injuries, and apixaban will be reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily. He was discharged home with his daughter with return precautions and follow-up in 1 week.

Denies headache, vomiting, neck pain, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness before the fall, new weakness, numbness, vision changes, abdominal pain and shortness of breath. History of atrial fibrillation, hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Also takes metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily. No known drug allergies.

Tender left parietal scalp hematoma about 3 cm without laceration or step-off; neurologic exam intact; no midline neck tenderness; 4 cm abrasion of the left forearm with mild distal radius tenderness and no deformity. CT head without contrast: no intracranial hemorrhage or fracture, scalp hematoma. CT cervical spine and left forearm and wrist X-ray: no fracture. ECG: atrial fibrillation, rate 78, no acute ischemia. Hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 1.6, potassium 4.2, troponin negative. Repeat CT head at 6 hours stable.

Hold apixaban tonight, then resume tomorrow morning at the reduced dose of 2.5 mg twice daily
Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain; avoid NSAIDs

Return for headache, vomiting, confusion, drowsiness or new weakness
Primary care follow-up in 1 week
Home physical therapy and home safety evaluation

note:
The patient is a 15-year-old male seen in the combined ear, nose, throat and eye clinic with his father for follow-up of chronic rhinosinusitis. He has had nasal congestion, thick yellow-green nasal drainage, postnasal drip, and a dull pressure sensation over both cheeks for more than 4 months, with worsening of the drainage over the past 10 days. He also reports itchy, watery eyes that are worse in the spring and a persistent cough at night that he attributes to the drainage. He denies fever, facial swelling, double vision, eye pain, and any change in his vision. There has been no nosebleed and no loss of smell. He has a history of allergic rhinitis and was started on loratadine 10 mg daily by his pediatrician last year, with limited benefit. He uses fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril daily but admits that he forgets doses about half of the time, and he does saline rinses only occasionally. He has no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature is 36.9 C, heart rate 72, blood pressure 112/68, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. Both eyes show mild conjunctival injection with a cobblestone appearance of the upper tarsal conjunctiva and clear watery discharge. The corneas are clear, the pupils are equal and reactive, and extraocular movements are full and painless. There is no periorbital edema or erythema. Anterior rhinoscopy shows pale, swollen inferior turbinates. Nasal endoscopy shows mucosal edema with mucopurulent secretions in the right middle meatus and no polyps or masses. There is mild tenderness over the maxillary sinuses, the oropharynx shows postnasal drainage without exudate, the ears are normal, and the neck has no adenopathy. A CT scan of the sinuses obtained last month showed bilateral maxillary and ethmoid mucosal thickening with partial opacification of the right maxillary sinus and no orbital involvement.

Impression is chronic rhinosinusitis with a purulent exacerbation, allergic rhinitis, and allergic conjunctivitis. We discussed that his symptoms are likely driven by untreated allergic inflammation plus inconsistent nasal steroid use. I recommended stopping loratadine and starting cetirizine 10 mg daily, continuing fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril daily with a routine tied to brushing his teeth, and starting olopatadine 0.2% ophthalmic solution one drop in each eye once daily. Because of the purulent secretions, I am starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily for 14 days. He will do saline sinus rinses twice daily. An allergy testing referral was placed, and we will repeat nasal endoscopy at the follow-up visit in 4 weeks. He should return sooner for fever, swelling around the eyes, vision changes, or severe headache. His father agreed with the plan.
summary: A 15-year-old male with allergic rhinitis was seen for chronic rhinosinusitis with more than 4 months of nasal congestion, thick nasal drainage and cheek pressure, worse over the past 10 days, along with itchy, watery eyes. Examination showed conjunctival injection, pale swollen turbinates and mucopurulent secretions in the right middle meatus on nasal endoscopy, and CT showed bilateral maxillary and ethmoid mucosal thickening. The impression is chronic rhinosinusitis with a purulent exacerbation, allergic rhinitis and allergic conjunctivitis. Loratadine was stopped in favor of cetirizine, and fluticasone nasal spray, olopatadine eye drops, amoxicillin-clavulanate for 14 days and saline rinses were prescribed, with allergy testing referral and a 4-week follow-up.

Mild maxillary sinus tenderness, postnasal drainage, normal ears, no adenopathy. CT of the sinuses: bilateral maxillary and ethmoid mucosal thickening with partial opacification of the right maxillary sinus, no orbital involvement.

note:
Doctor: Good morning, thanks for coming in. I have your chart here. You're a 35-year-old male, and I understand you were in the hospital recently and they found something on your lung scan?
Patient: Yes, I was in the hospital about three weeks ago with pneumonia. They did a CT scan of my chest and the radiologist said there's a small spot on my right lung, and honestly I've been pretty worried since.
Doctor: That's understandable. How are you feeling now compared with when you were admitted?
Patient: Much better. The fever is gone and the cough is mostly gone, just a little tickle in the morning.
Doctor: Any coughing up blood, chest pain, shortness of breath, or weight loss?
Patient: No blood, no chest pain, no trouble breathing, and no weight loss. No night sweats either.
Doctor: Good. Do you smoke or vape, or have you ever?
Patient: Never smoked, never vaped. I work in an office. No asbestos or anything like that.
Doctor: Any family history of lung cancer?
Patient: No, my dad has high blood pressure and that's about it. I do have seasonal allergies and I take cetirizine 10 mg most mornings in the spring.
Doctor: What did they send you home on?
Patient: An antibiotic called amoxicillin-clavulanate, 875 milligrams twice a day for seven days, and I finished that last week. They also gave me an albuterol inhaler to use if I was coughing, two puffs every six hours as needed, but I haven't used it in over a week.
Doctor: Perfect. Your vitals today are blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 68, temperature 36.7 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. I listened to your lungs and they sound clear on both sides, no wheezes or crackles. I also reviewed the hospital CT. It shows a solid nodule in the right upper lobe measuring 6 millimeters, and the pneumonia in the right lower lobe is mostly resolved. We did spirometry today and it was normal, with an FEV1 of 98 percent of predicted.
Patient: So is it cancer?
Doctor: With a nodule this small in a young nonsmoker, the chance of cancer is very low. It may well be a leftover inflammatory spot from the pneumonia. The guideline approach is to recheck with a CT. Since you just had pneumonia, I'd like to repeat a low-dose CT of the chest in three months so the pneumonia changes have cleared and we can measure the nodule cleanly, and then again at 12 months if it is unchanged.
Patient: Okay. Should I keep the inhaler?
Doctor: You don't need it, so please stop the albuterol, and keep taking your cetirizine as you have been. Call us if you start coughing up blood, have a fever, or lose weight without trying. Otherwise we'll see you right after the CT in three months.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
summary: A 35-year-old male never-smoker was seen for follow-up of an incidental lung nodule found on a chest CT during a hospitalization for pneumonia about three weeks ago. He has only a mild morning cough tickle now, with no hemoptysis, chest pain, trouble breathing, weight loss or night sweats. Vitals and lung examination were normal, spirometry was normal, and the hospital CT showed a 6 millimeter solid nodule in the right upper lobe with the pneumonia mostly resolved. The nodule is considered very low risk and possibly inflammatory. A low-dose chest CT is planned in three months, with another at 12 months if unchanged, and albuterol was stopped while cetirizine continues.

soap.subjective: 35-year-old male hospitalized about three weeks ago with pneumonia; a chest CT during the stay showed a small spot on the right lung. Now much better, fever gone, cough mostly gone with just a little tickle in the morning. Denies coughing up blood, chest pain, trouble breathing, weight loss and night sweats. Never smoked or vaped, works in an office, no asbestos exposure, no family history of lung cancer. Has seasonal allergies and takes cetirizine 10 mg most mornings in the spring. Finished amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice a day for seven days last week. Was given albuterol, two puffs every six hours as needed, but has not used it in over a week.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 68, temperature 36.7 Celsius, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Lungs clear on both sides with no wheezes or crackles. Hospital CT shows a solid nodule in the right upper lobe measuring 6 millimeters, with the right lower lobe pneumonia mostly resolved. Spirometry normal with FEV1 98 percent of predicted.
soap.assessment: Incidental 6 millimeter solid nodule in the right upper lobe in a young nonsmoker, very low chance of cancer and possibly an inflammatory leftover from the pneumonia. Recent pneumonia, mostly resolved. Seasonal allergies.
plan: Repeat low-dose CT of the chest in three months, then again at 12 months if the nodule is unchanged
Stop albuterol
Continue cetirizine
Call for coughing up blood, fever or unintentional weight loss
Follow up right after the CT in three months

note:
Doctor: Hi, what brings you to urgent care today?
Patient: I've had watery diarrhea for three days, about six times a day, with a lot of belly cramping. I'm worried the C. diff is back.
Doctor: You're a 36-year-old male, and you had C. diff before, right?
Patient: Yes, about two months ago I got it after some antibiotics for a tooth infection. They gave me vancomycin 125 milligrams four times a day for ten days and I got better, but now it's back.
Doctor: Any blood in the stool, fever, or vomiting?
Patient: No blood, no fever, and no vomiting. I'm drinking fine.
Doctor: Good. Your vitals are normal today, temperature 36.9 Celsius, heart rate 84, blood pressure 122/76. Your belly is soft with mild tenderness all over and no guarding or rebound. Given your history, this looks like a recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, your first recurrence. I'm sending a stool C. diff test now, and I'm going to start fidaxomicin 200 milligrams twice daily for 10 days, since it lowers the chance of another recurrence compared with vancomycin. Stay hydrated, avoid antidiarrheal medicines, wash your hands with soap and water, and avoid any unnecessary antibiotics. I'll also refer you to the infectious disease clinic to talk about options if it comes back.
Patient: Okay, how soon should I feel better?
Doctor: Usually within two to three days. Come back or go to the ER if you have blood in the stool, a fever, severe belly pain, or you can't keep fluids down.
Patient: Got it, thanks.
summary: A 36-year-old male presented to urgent care with three days of watery diarrhea about six times a day and belly cramping, two months after treatment for Clostridioides difficile with vancomycin. He denies blood in the stool, fever and vomiting. Vitals were normal and the abdomen was soft with mild diffuse tenderness and no guarding or rebound. The impression is a first recurrence of Clostridioides difficile infection. A stool test was sent, fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days was started, and he was advised on hydration, hand washing, avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and an infectious disease referral.

soap.subjective: 36-year-old male with three days of watery diarrhea about six times a day and a lot of belly cramping. Had C. diff about two months ago after antibiotics for a tooth infection and was treated with vancomycin 125 milligrams four times a day for ten days with improvement. Denies blood in the stool, fever and vomiting, and is drinking fine.
soap.objective: Temperature 36.9 Celsius, heart rate 84, blood pressure 122/76. Abdomen soft with mild tenderness all over and no guarding or rebound.
soap.assessment: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, first recurrence.
plan: Send stool C. diff test
Start fidaxomicin 200 milligrams twice daily for 10 days
Stay hydrated, avoid antidiarrheal medicines, wash hands with soap and water, avoid unnecessary antibiotics
Refer to the infectious disease clinic to discuss options if it recurs
Return or go to the ER for blood in the stool, fever, severe belly pain or inability to keep fluids down

note:
Hospital day 3 progress note for an 80-year-old male admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis in the setting of type 2 diabetes mellitus. He had been rationing his insulin for several weeks because he could not afford it. He presented with vomiting and marked thirst. This morning he reports feeling much better and denies nausea, abdominal pain, and chest pain, and he ate a full breakfast. The insulin infusion was stopped yesterday evening after the anion gap closed, with the first subcutaneous dose given before the infusion was discontinued. Current regimen is insulin glargine 20 units nightly and insulin lispro 6 units with meals.

Vitals are temperature 36.8 Celsius, heart rate 82, blood pressure 130/76, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Exam shows moist mucous membranes, a soft nontender abdomen, and clear lungs. Morning labs show glucose 168, potassium 4.0, bicarbonate 24, and anion gap 10, and the beta-hydroxybutyrate has normalized. Creatinine is 1.1 and is back at his baseline.

Assessment is diabetic ketoacidosis, resolved, precipitated by insulin non-adherence due to cost. Plan is to continue insulin glargine 20 units nightly and insulin lispro 6 units with meals, check fingerstick glucose before meals and at bedtime, and obtain a hemoglobin A1c. A social work and pharmacy consult has been placed to enroll him in an insulin cost-assistance program and identify a lower-cost insulin option before discharge. Diabetes education was completed, including sick-day rules and never stopping basal insulin. Anticipate discharge tomorrow with primary care follow-up in one week.
summary: An 80-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus is on hospital day 3 after admission with diabetic ketoacidosis caused by rationing insulin because of cost. He now feels much better and denies nausea, abdominal pain and chest pain. Vitals are stable, the anion gap has closed, glucose is 168 and creatinine is back at baseline. The assessment is resolved diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by cost-related insulin non-adherence. He will continue insulin glargine and insulin lispro, have a hemoglobin A1c checked, and receive social work and pharmacy help with insulin costs before discharge tomorrow.

Glucose 168, potassium 4.0, bicarbonate 24, anion gap 10, beta-hydroxybutyrate normalized, creatinine 1.1 at baseline.
soap.assessment: Diabetic ketoacidosis, resolved, precipitated by insulin non-adherence due to cost. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Fingerstick glucose before meals and at bedtime

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. You're a 64-year-old female here for your COPD follow-up, correct? How have you been since the last visit?
Patient: Not great, honestly. I get winded going up one flight of stairs, and I'm coughing every morning with some white phlegm. This past winter I had two bad flare-ups.
Doctor: Tell me about those flare-ups.
Patient: The first one in November, my cough got worse and the phlegm turned yellow, and my primary doctor gave me steroids and an antibiotic. The second one was in February, same thing, same treatment. I wasn't in the hospital either time.
Doctor: Any fever, chest pain, leg swelling, or coughing up blood?
Patient: No fever. No chest pain. No swelling in my legs. And no blood when I cough.
Doctor: What inhalers are you using now?
Patient: I use the Anoro, one puff every morning, and my albuterol inhaler, two puffs when I'm short of breath, which is maybe four or five times a day lately. I also take amlodipine 5 mg every day for my high blood pressure.
Doctor: Do you still smoke?
Patient: I do, about ten cigarettes a day. I've smoked since I was eighteen. I know I should quit.
Doctor: I appreciate you being honest, and we'll talk about that. Let me go over your numbers. Blood pressure is 142/84, heart rate 88, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Your lungs show diminished breath sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase and no wheezes, and there is no leg edema. Your spirometry today shows an FEV1 of 52 percent of predicted and an FEV1 to FVC ratio of 0.58, so you have moderate to severe COPD. With two flare-ups in a year and ongoing symptoms, the Anoro isn't enough. I'd like to stop it and switch you to Trelegy Ellipta, one inhalation once daily, which adds an inhaled steroid. Keep the albuterol for rescue, and rinse your mouth after each use of the Trelegy.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: For smoking, I recommend a nicotine patch, 14 mg every 24 hours, to start. Quitting is the single most important thing we can do to slow this down. I'm also ordering a low-dose CT scan of the chest for lung cancer screening, referring you to pulmonary rehab, and recommending a pneumococcal vaccine and a flu shot this fall. Let's see you again in three months.
Patient: I'll try the patch.
summary: A 64-year-old female current smoker with COPD presented for follow-up with exertional breathlessness, a daily morning cough with white phlegm, and two flare-ups this past winter treated as an outpatient. She denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling and coughing up blood. Spirometry showed an FEV1 of 52 percent of predicted with a ratio of 0.58, oxygen saturation was 93% on room air, and breath sounds were diminished. The assessment is moderate to severe COPD with frequent flare-ups on current therapy. Anoro was stopped and switched to Trelegy Ellipta, a nicotine patch was started, and a low-dose chest CT, pulmonary rehab and vaccines were arranged with follow-up in three months.

soap.subjective: 64-year-old female with COPD here for follow-up. Gets winded going up one flight of stairs and coughs every morning with some white phlegm. Denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling and coughing up blood. Uses Anoro one puff every morning, albuterol two puffs when short of breath about four or five times a day lately, and amlodipine 5 mg every day for high blood pressure. Currently smokes about ten cigarettes a day since age eighteen.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 142/84, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Diminished breath sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase, no wheezes, no leg edema. Spirometry: FEV1 52 percent of predicted, FEV1 to FVC ratio 0.58.
soap.assessment: Moderate to severe COPD with two flare-ups in a year and ongoing symptoms on Anoro. High blood pressure. Current smoking.
plan: Stop Anoro and switch to Trelegy Ellipta, one inhalation once daily; rinse mouth after each use
Continue albuterol for rescue
Continue amlodipine 5 mg every day
Start nicotine patch 14 mg every 24 hours and counsel on quitting smoking
Low-dose CT scan of the chest for lung cancer screening
Refer to pulmonary rehab
Pneumococcal vaccine and flu shot this fall
Follow up in three months

note:
The patient is a 44-year-old male seen in the family medicine clinic for 12 days of nasal congestion and facial pain. He is accompanied by his sister, who helps manage his medications and provided part of the history because of his memory difficulties after a traumatic brain injury several years ago. They report that he had a typical cold at the start, began to improve around day 5, and then worsened again over the last 4 days with thick yellow nasal drainage, pressure and pain over the right cheek and upper teeth, a fever of 38.2 Celsius at home, and a headache that is worse when he bends forward. The patient himself says the headache is moderate and the pain is mostly on the right side. His sister has been giving him pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 6 hours and oxymetazoline nasal spray for the past 6 days. He and his sister both deny vision changes, swelling around the eyes, stiff neck, confusion beyond his baseline, shortness of breath, and chest pain.

Past medical history includes T2DM, HTN, hyperlipidemia, and a traumatic brain injury (TBI) with mild memory impairment. His sister initially stated that he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily, but after checking the bottles she brought with her, she clarified that the dose is lisinopril 20 mg daily. Other regular medications are metformin 500 mg BID, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. He also takes several over-the-counter supplements: vitamin D3 2000 units daily and fish oil 1000 mg daily, and for this illness he has been taking echinacea capsules and zinc lozenges. He has a sulfa antibiotic allergy that causes a rash. He does not smoke and drinks alcohol rarely.

On examination, temperature is 38.0 Celsius, heart rate 96, blood pressure 158/94, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and at his baseline orientation. There is tenderness to percussion over the right maxillary sinus, purulent drainage in the right nasal passage with swollen turbinates, and mild erythema of the posterior pharynx with postnasal drainage. The tympanic membranes are normal, there is no periorbital edema, the neck is supple, the lungs are clear, and the heart is regular. POC testing showed a hemoglobin A1c of 8.2%, and clinic labs show glucose 182, creatinine 0.9, eGFR 96, and potassium 4.1.

Impression is acute bacterial sinusitis, since symptoms have persisted beyond 10 days with a double worsening pattern and fever. His blood pressure is elevated, most likely from the pseudoephedrine, and his diabetes is above goal. We explained to the patient and his sister that decongestants raise blood pressure and can worsen blood sugar. Plan is to stop the pseudoephedrine and the oxymetazoline spray immediately. Start amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg BID for 7 days with food, which is safe with his documented sulfa allergy. Start fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril once daily and saline nasal irrigation twice daily. Increase metformin from 500 mg BID to 1000 mg BID with meals, and continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. He may continue vitamin D3 and fish oil but should stop the echinacea, which has no proven benefit. Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours PRN for pain. Recheck blood pressure and review his home glucose log in 1 week, and call sooner if there is no improvement in 3 days. If symptoms worsen, we will consider a CT of the sinuses. His sister will use a weekly pill organizer and keep an updated medication list. Return precautions were reviewed, including severe headache, vision changes, eye swelling, or confusion, and both the patient and his sister verbalized understanding.

Pseudoephedrine and oxymetazoline were stopped, amoxicillin-clavulanate and fluticasone nasal spray were started, and metformin was increased to 1000 mg BID with follow-up in 1 week.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I see you're a 91-year-old male, and you're here to talk about your bone health after the wrist fracture?
Patient: Yes. About two months ago I slipped on the kitchen floor and put my hand out, and they said I broke my wrist. My daughter thought I should have my bones checked.
Doctor: That's smart. A broken wrist from a fall from standing height is what we call a fragility fracture, and it's a strong sign of thin bones. Have you had any other fractures, back pain, or more falls since then?
Patient: No other broken bones, no back pain, and no more falls. I use a cane now.
Doctor: Good. Any trouble swallowing or heartburn?
Patient: No, nothing like that. I eat fine.
Doctor: Your bone density scan last week showed a T-score of minus 3.1 at the hip, which confirms osteoporosis. Your kidney function from the blood work is fine, with a creatinine of 1.0, your calcium is normal, and your vitamin D level is low at 18. Blood pressure today is 134/78.
Patient: So what do I do about it?
Doctor: I recommend starting alendronate 70 milligrams once a week. You take it first thing in the morning with a full glass of plain water, and you stay upright for at least 30 minutes before eating. I also want you to start vitamin D3 1000 units daily and eat calcium-rich foods. We'll also set up a home safety check and balance exercises with physical therapy to prevent falls.
Patient: Okay, I can do that.
Doctor: Come back in three months and we'll check how you're tolerating it.
summary: A 91-year-old male was seen for bone health after breaking his wrist in a fall from standing height about two months ago. He denies other fractures, back pain, more falls, trouble swallowing and heartburn. Bone density testing showed a hip T-score of minus 3.1, his creatinine is 1.0 and calcium is normal, but vitamin D is low at 18. The assessment is osteoporosis after a fragility fracture. Alendronate 70 mg once a week and vitamin D3 1000 units daily were started, with a home safety check, balance exercises with physical therapy and follow-up in three months.

soap.assessment: Osteoporosis confirmed after a fragility fracture of the wrist. Low vitamin D.

note:
Doctor: Hello, I understand you're an 82-year-old female coming in about your headaches. Tell me what's been happening.
Patient: I've had migraines since I was in my twenties, always with those zigzag lines in my vision, but lately they've been coming almost every week instead of once a month.
Doctor: Describe a typical one.
Patient: First I see shimmering zigzag lines on the left side of my vision for about twenty minutes. Then a throbbing headache comes on behind my right eye, with nausea, and light bothers me. It lasts most of the day.
Doctor: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or loss of vision that lasts beyond the zigzags?
Patient: No weakness, no numbness, and no trouble speaking. My vision comes back to normal after the aura.
Doctor: Any jaw pain when you chew, scalp tenderness, or fever?
Patient: No jaw pain, no scalp tenderness, and no fever.
Doctor: What do you take for them?
Patient: Sumatriptan 50 mg when it starts, and sometimes ibuprofen 400 mg. I also take amlodipine 5 mg daily for my blood pressure.
Doctor: And do you smoke?
Patient: Yes, about half a pack a day for sixty years.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. Today your blood pressure is 148/84 and your heart rate is 70. Your neurologic exam is normal, with cranial nerves, strength, sensation, reflexes and gait all intact, and there is no temporal artery tenderness. This is migraine with aura with a recent increase in frequency. Because you're over 65, you smoke, and you have high blood pressure, sumatriptan raises the risk of stroke and heart problems, so I'd like you to stop it, and stop the ibuprofen as well. I'm prescribing rimegepant 75 mg, one dissolving tablet at the start of a headache, no more than one dose in 24 hours. You can use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours if needed. Because of the change in pattern and your age, I'm also ordering an MRI of the brain and blood tests for ESR and CRP. Please work on quitting smoking, which raises your stroke risk with migraine aura, and I'd be glad to help with that. Let's follow up in six weeks.
Patient: Okay, I'll try.
summary: An 82-year-old female smoker with long-standing migraine with aura reports that her headaches have increased from monthly to almost weekly, with shimmering zigzag lines lasting about twenty minutes followed by a throbbing headache, nausea and light sensitivity. She denies weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, jaw pain, scalp tenderness and fever. Blood pressure was 148/84 and the neurologic exam was normal with no temporal artery tenderness. The assessment is migraine with aura with a recent increase in frequency, and sumatriptan is unsafe given her age, smoking and high blood pressure. Sumatriptan and ibuprofen were stopped, rimegepant and acetaminophen were prescribed, an MRI of the brain, ESR and CRP were ordered, and smoking cessation was advised.

note: Dictating an eye clinic visit for a 67-year-old male with a red eye. He reports that his left eye, correction, his right eye, became red and watery 2 days ago with crusting of the lashes in the morning, and now the left eye is starting to feel scratchy as well. His grandchild had pink eye last week. He denies eye pain, vision changes, light sensitivity, and thick discharge, and he does not wear contact lenses. His only medical history is hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies. On examination visual acuity is 20/25 in each eye without correction. There is diffuse conjunctival injection of the right eye greater than the left with watery discharge and a palpable right preauricular lymph node. The corneas are clear with no uptake on fluorescein staining, the pupils are equal and reactive, and the anterior chamber is quiet on slit lamp examination. Impression is acute viral conjunctivitis, likely adenoviral. Plan is supportive care with artificial tears one drop in each eye four times daily as needed and cold compresses. No antibiotic drops because this is viral. Strict hand hygiene and no sharing of towels. Continue lisinopril. Follow up in one week if not improving, or sooner for pain, vision loss, or light sensitivity.

Visual acuity was 20/25 in each eye, with conjunctival injection and watery discharge, a palpable right preauricular lymph node, clear corneas without fluorescein uptake and a quiet anterior chamber. The impression is acute viral conjunctivitis, likely adenoviral. Management is supportive with artificial tears and cold compresses, no antibiotic drops, hand hygiene, continued lisinopril and follow-up in one week if not improving.

note:
Visit modality: telephone visit (audio only) with the patient at home. The patient confirmed his identity and consented to a telephone visit. No visual examination was possible.

Reason for visit: follow-up of nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy. The patient is a 42-year-old male with membranous nephropathy diagnosed on kidney biopsy 3 months ago, with positive anti-PLA2R antibodies. He also has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a left leg deep vein thrombosis diagnosed 2 months ago for which he takes apixaban. The patient sounded anxious throughout the call and asked many questions, including whether he will need dialysis, whether the swelling means his heart is failing, whether his blood thinner will cause bleeding, and whether he can keep taking ibuprofen for aches. Each question was answered in turn.

History per patient: ankle and leg swelling has been getting worse over the past 2 weeks, with foamy urine, weight gain, and mild fatigue. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, calf pain, blood in his urine, black stools, gum bleeding, and decreased urine output. He first stated that he takes apixaban 5 mg once daily, but when asked to read the bottle he clarified that it is 5 mg BID and that he has not missed any doses. He has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg about three times a week for back aches. His other medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements: BP 148/92 on his home cuff, average of two readings this morning, heart rate 78, pulse oximeter reading 98%, and weight 212 pounds compared with 204 pounds two weeks ago.

Labs from last week were reviewed with him: urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 7.2 g/g, serum albumin 2.4 g/dL, creatinine 1.1 with an eGFR of 82, potassium 4.3, and LDL cholesterol 172.

Impression: nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy with persistent heavy proteinuria and volume overload, hypertension above goal, and hyperlipidemia. The DVT is being treated with apixaban and there is no sign of bleeding. His preserved kidney function and low risk of dialysis in the near term were explained, and he was reassured that the swelling is from protein loss rather than heart failure, which does not rule out a cardiac evaluation if symptoms change. The risk of bleeding with apixaban was reviewed, along with the reason to avoid NSAIDs.

Management: stop ibuprofen and avoid all NSAIDs, and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours PRN for aches instead. Increase lisinopril from 20 mg to 40 mg daily to reduce proteinuria and blood pressure. Continue furosemide 40 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg BID without any change, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. Follow a 2 gram sodium diet and weigh himself every morning. Basic metabolic panel in 1 week to check potassium and creatinine after the lisinopril increase. Repeat urine protein-to-creatinine ratio and serum albumin in 4 weeks, and if proteinuria remains heavy we will discuss immunosuppressive therapy such as rituximab after hepatitis B serology. He was encouraged to write down further questions and call the clinic nurse line with them. Return precautions reviewed, including chest pain, shortness of breath, calf swelling or pain, or any bleeding. Telephone follow-up in 2 weeks. The call lasted 28 minutes.
summary: A 42-year-old male with membranous nephropathy, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and a left leg deep vein thrombosis on apixaban had a telephone follow-up for nephrotic syndrome, with worsening ankle and leg swelling, foamy urine and weight gain, and he was anxious and asked many questions. Home blood pressure was 148/92 and weight was up 8 pounds, and labs showed a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 7.2 g/g, albumin 2.4 g/dL and LDL 172. The impression is nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy with volume overload, hypertension above goal and hyperlipidemia. Ibuprofen was stopped, lisinopril was increased from 20 mg to 40 mg daily, and a basic metabolic panel, repeat proteinuria testing and telephone follow-up were arranged.

note:
Dictating a rheumatology clinic note on a 25-year-old male seen for acute pain and swelling of the right big toe. Onset was overnight 2 days ago. He woke with severe throbbing pain in the right first metatarsophalangeal joint that was so intense that even the bedsheet touching it hurt, and the joint became red and swollen by morning. This followed a weekend of heavy beer drinking and a large meal of red meat and shellfish. He has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours with only partial relief. He denies fever, chills, rash, and pain in other joints, and he has never had a kidney stone. He had one similar, milder episode in the left ankle last year that resolved on its own. His father has gout. He takes no other medications and has no known drug allergies.

Vitals, temperature 37.2 Celsius, heart rate 84, blood pressure 132/84, and BMI 31, so he has obesity. On examination the right first MTP joint is swollen, erythematous, warm, and exquisitely tender to light touch with limited range of motion. No tophi are seen, the other joints are normal without synovitis, and there is no skin breakdown or lymphangitic streaking. Arthrocentesis of the right first MTP was performed with sterile technique and returned cloudy fluid, and polarized light microscopy showed needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals consistent with monosodium urate, with a synovial white count of 22,000 and a negative Gram stain. Serum uric acid is 9.8, correction, 9.3 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0, and eGFR 105. X-ray of the right foot shows soft tissue swelling without erosions.

Impression is acute gout flare of the right first MTP, podagra, confirmed by crystal analysis, with hyperuricemia and obesity. Plan is to stop ibuprofen and start naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for 7 days, with ice and rest of the foot. He was counseled to limit beer, red meat, and shellfish, avoid sugary drinks, and work on weight loss. Since he is young with a high uric acid level and now a second episode, we will discuss urate-lowering therapy at follow-up once the flare has resolved. We will recheck uric acid, liver function tests, and a lipid panel at the follow-up visit in 2 weeks. He should return sooner for fever or if the joint is not improving within 48 hours. End of dictation.
summary: A 25-year-old male with obesity presented with 2 days of severe throbbing pain, redness and swelling of the right big toe after heavy beer and red meat intake, with only partial relief from ibuprofen. The right first MTP joint was swollen, warm and exquisitely tender, and arthrocentesis showed needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals with a synovial white count of 22,000, while serum uric acid was 9.3 mg/dL. The impression is an acute gout flare with hyperuricemia and obesity. Ibuprofen was stopped and naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 7 days was started with ice, dietary counseling and follow-up in 2 weeks to discuss urate-lowering therapy.

note:
Hospital day 3 progress note for a 91-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury due to dehydration.

Overnight events and interval history: She was admitted after 4 days of poor oral intake, watery stools that have now stopped, and lightheadedness on standing. She had also been drinking a dandelion herbal tea several times a day for leg swelling, in addition to her prescribed furosemide. Overnight she had no fever, no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no vomiting, and no diarrhea since yesterday. She says she feels less dizzy today and drank 600 mL of fluid yesterday. Her daughter reports that the patient also takes over-the-counter supplements: vitamin D3 1000 units daily, a calcium carbonate tablet, and turmeric capsules 500 mg twice daily.

Past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, HTN, T2DM, CKD stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of 1.0, and HFpEF. On admission her apixaban dose was recorded as 2.5 mg twice daily, correction, the pharmacy fill history confirms she was taking 5 mg twice daily. She has no known drug allergies.

Current medications and infusions: lactated Ringer's at 75 mL per hour, insulin lispro on a sliding scale before meals, apixaban, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and vitamin D3 1000 units daily. Held since admission are lisinopril 20 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. The turmeric and the dandelion herbal tea have been stopped.

Vitals and data: temperature 36.6 Celsius, heart rate 74, blood pressure 112/64 lying and 104/60 standing, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, weight 52 kg compared with 51 kg on admission. Net intake exceeded output by 1.1 L over the last 24 hours, with urine output of 0.8 mL/kg/hr. Creatinine was 2.4 on admission, 1.9 yesterday, and 1.6 today. BUN has improved from 52 to 38. Sodium was 148 on admission and is 142 today, potassium is 3.8, and bicarbonate is 22. Hemoglobin is 11.4. Urinalysis was bland with no protein or blood, and urine sodium was low. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.

Exam: frail elderly woman, comfortable, alert and oriented. Mucous membranes are now moist and skin turgor has improved. JVP is not elevated, the heart is irregularly irregular without murmur, the lungs are clear with no crackles, the abdomen is soft, and there is no leg edema and no costovertebral angle tenderness.

Acute kidney injury, prerenal from dehydration (poor oral intake, watery stools, diuretic, and herbal diuretic tea), improving with creatinine down from 2.4 to 1.6. Doctor: Good morning, welcome in. You're a 20-year-old male coming in for your annual physical and to catch up on vaccines, right?
Patient: Yeah, I'm a college student and my school wants my records updated.
Doctor: Great. How have you been feeling overall? Any new problems?
Patient: Pretty good. I get pimples on my face and back, and I've been on doxycycline 100 milligrams twice a day for acne for about four months. It's helped a lot.
Doctor: Good. Any stomach upset or sun problems with it?
Patient: No stomach upset and no sunburns beyond normal.
Doctor: And your asthma? I see mild intermittent asthma in your chart.
Patient: It's been fine. I use my albuterol inhaler, two puffs, only when I play basketball in the cold, maybe once or twice a month. No wheezing or cough lately, and no waking up at night.
Doctor: Any chest pain or fainting with exercise?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: How's your mood and sleep?
Patient: Fine, just a bit tired during finals.
Doctor: Do you smoke, vape, or drink?
Patient: No smoking or vaping. I have a couple of beers on weekends.
Doctor: Okay. Vitals today: blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 66, and your BMI is 23.8. Peak flow was 620 liters per minute, which is normal for you. Your PHQ-9 depression screen scored 1. Heart sounds normal, lungs clear with no wheezes, and your skin shows mild acne on the face and upper back with no cysts.
Patient: Sounds good. What about the vaccines?
Doctor: You had your childhood series, and Tdap at age eleven, so the next booster isn't due for several years. You had one HPV shot at age 14, so you need a second dose to finish the series. You also had your meningococcal ACWY shot at eleven but no booster, and since you live in the dorms, you should get the booster today. And it's flu season, so I recommend a flu shot too.
Patient: Fine, all three today.
Doctor: Great. For the acne, since four months of doxycycline has helped, I'd like to stop the doxycycline now to avoid long-term antibiotic use and switch you to adapalene 0.1% gel at night on the face and upper back, with sunscreen. Keep the albuterol as needed. I'll also order screening bloodwork for HIV and hepatitis C, which is recommended once for everyone your age. Come back in a year, or sooner if the acne flares.
Patient: Okay, thanks.
summary: A 20-year-old male college student with acne and mild intermittent asthma came for an annual preventive visit and vaccine update. He denies wheezing, cough, night waking, chest pain and fainting, does not smoke or vape, and has had good control with albuterol only before exercise in the cold. Vitals and examination were normal apart from mild acne, peak flow was 620 liters per minute and the PHQ-9 score was 1. He received the second HPV dose, a meningococcal ACWY booster and a flu shot, doxycycline was stopped and adapalene gel started for acne, and screening bloodwork for HIV and hepatitis C was ordered with follow-up in a year.
